title: Project resources
text:
This page is a collection of resources that are used regularly to annotate sound files for orthopterans. Since a lot of the bioacoustics information for orthopterans is split up across online resources, annotators should use all of these links as needed. The best workflow will start with the first two resources listed and continue to others if doubt still remains about the song in question. Using all the available information provided by these resources, annotators should then make an informed decision.

1. Orthoptera Song Guide
This guide details all the possible species that occur in our sampling region along with their frequency range, signal morphology, and links to example recordings. This guide should be used every time an Orthopteran is identified in this project.


2. Singing Insects of North America (SINA)
SINA is the main resource used in the Orthoptera Song Guide. It will have examples and/or information for all the species in the sampling region. Other resources might not have a full record, but for some species other resources might provide valuable alternative examples to SINA and/or necessary information to make a proper ID.


3. Song of Insects
Song of Insects is an online database with the most common species. This database often has acoustic-specific information which SINA sometimes does not, as well as more examples of song patterns—sometimes recorded in the field. This can be useful to compare the variation between different resources and our field recordings.


4. Xeno Canto
Xeno Canto is the best resource for field recordings but might not have all the species in the sampling region. Also, since Xeno Canto is a community science database the recording examples will be biased towards popular and common species.


5. Nature Inquiries
Nature inquiries is a great place to read naturalist notes that don’t appear in any of the other reference links. Specifically, most submissions are natural history notes about sound descriptions, anecdotyl observations, and help separating like-sounding species of singing insects. The site is run by Dr. Carl Strang, who resides in Illinois and is dedicated to collecting and sharing natural history accounts about singing insects. His data contributions and notes on this website have helped me insurmountably throughout this project. The only downside being that the species discussed on this page are mostly from Illinois, so they need to share a geographic range with Texas. Search the name of the species in the search bar or in a search engine followed by “Nature Inquiries”.


6. Listening to Insects
This is a go-to for a second opinion or supplementary information. The species list is limited, but it is useful especially for seperating the trilling trigs and ground crickets. The only downside being that the species discussed on this page are mostly from Illinois, so they need to share a geographic range with ohio.


7. Orthoptera of North Carolina
Another great resource that sometimes has more information about chirp and pulse rates, and some different reference recordings than SINA or Song of Insects. Species listed on this site are from North Carolina, so they need to share a geographic range with Texas.

title: ID Help | Blog
text:
*audio coming soon*
Orthopterans are deceivingly difficult to identify by sound. They are easy to annotate, because often their songs carry across an entire recording when viewed in sound analysis software like RavenPro. At least in our recording for eastern Texas, there are often only 1-2 species occupying a given frequency niche (less noise and other taxa vocalizing at night). Species identification, however, is a different story. Unlike birds, many orthopterans seemingly share the same song. Between like-species the only identifiable information is typically buried in the frequency range, note morphology, chirp rate, or pulse rate of the species. I found it quite difficult to find this information in a single location. Rather, bioacoustics information for Orthoptera was spread across different online resources.
My hope is that this page will act as a resource for annotators on this project. The page is a simplified collection of my notes supported by other resources which are used to identify like-sounding Orthoptera species in eastern Texas.
Note: mp3 examples coming soon. Embedding audio into Quarto websites is weird, and maybe impossible? TBD.

Trilling Oecanthus | Neoscapteriscus borellii
Just a refresher that the annotation tables for this project are set up with a Annotation column which gets the primary ID, and a Notes column which gets the secondary ID (if applicable).
N. borelli (Southern mole cricket) and trilling Oecanthus (tree crickets) below 3 kHz should always be included as the alternative ID and vice versa. For the purposes of this project their song is too similar to reliably provide a single ID, and they have very little information available that separates the two species at the resolution that we work with.
Trilling Oecanthus is much more common than N. borelli in the project recordings and should be receiving the primary ID most of the time. There are many co-occurring species in genus Oecanthus, each with minor differences in their song. Regardless, here are some clues that N. borelli could be singing:
N. borelli is somewhat frog-like, and sounds like a “small mower” on the woodland floor or is described as very bass-heavy. Oecanthus is more chime-like and melodic, however O. exclamationis does sound quite bass-heavy to me, but not as much as N. borelli . Oecanthus will often chorus in a continuous trill at a standard frequency. Multiple N. borelli might call at once, but with distinct differences likely present on the spectrogram because of the way that they project their calls. The morphology of their burrows act as a bugle for their calls to project across the soundscape which may cause slightly overlapped signals within 0.1-0.2 kHz of a single frequency range.
N. borelli will not deviate from a carrier frequency of 2.5-2.7 kHz. The latter is not helpful since Oecanthus exclamationis occupies this frequency range as well. Likewise, the pulse rates differ but our recordings are not of high enough resolution to parse apart most pulse rates in trills (~50-70 p/ch). Supposedly N. borelli will only sing during the first hour or two after sunset.
Summary: It will be Oecanthus 99% of the time from my experience, but technically there could be a chance that it is N. borelli if the song is under 2.9-3 kHz. I don’t have good enough ears to parse the songs apart, and the pulse rate is too difficult to view at our resolution.


Trilling Oecanthus | Gryllus rubens 
Trilling Oecanthus and Gryllus can be reliably seperated by sound. The song of Gryllus rubens (Southeastern field cricket) is much drier than Oecanthus (tree crickets), which is more melodic and chime-like. The signal of Gryllus rubens is more broadband—appearing as little slivers (Fig 1). The Oecanthus signal is a single thin, often muffled continuous line of sound. The signal morphology might be masked by background noise, which is why the sound (dry versus melodic) should be used as well.



Fig 1. The stidulation pattern of Gryllus rubens.





Fig 2. The stridulation pattern of three individual trilling species in the genus Oecanthus. Notice the difference in signal morphology when compared to G. rubens.




Oecanthus fultoni | Velarifictorus micado | Gryllus fultoni
Oh boy… this one gave me a headache. The SINA reference recording makes Velarifictorus micado (Japanese burrowing cricket) sound very similar to Oecanthus fultoni (Snowy tree cricket) but this is rarely the case. I think the recordings are just short enough to mask the characteristic tells of V. micado, and a fast chirping O. fultoni. Nowhere does it discuss these two species sounding similar. Instead, V. micado and Gryllus fultoni (Southern wood cricket) are discussed as like-sounding species. It wasn’t until I came across our own recordings that were so obviously V. micado that I started to piece together the reliable information for ID.
Due to the variability in O. fultoni ’s song (Snowy tree cricket, aka the temperature cricket), these three species can occur very close in the frequency niche space. I’ve found that between V. micado and O. fultoni the note morphology looks similar.



Fig 3. A spectrogram showing songs from V. micado (top), and O. fultoni (bottom).


I’ve found that O. fultoni gives a consistent and slightly melodic chirp, rarely breaking it’s tempo. V. micado’s tempo is FAST. However, this is not enough for an ID, since technically O. fultoni can reach a similar ch/s rate under high temperatures. Characteristically the tempo of V. micado is regularly tripping over itself—starting and stopping continuously in one bout of song, which I haven’t found O. fultoni to do in our recordings or any reference recordings. Also, V. micado’s chirp is drier than O. fultoni, sounding closer to Gryllus than Oecanthus.
That being said, checking historical weather data can’t hurt. Fahrenheit temperature can be estimated by counting the chirps in 13 sec. and adding 40. for the O. fultoni. As far as I know, as an ectotherm V. micado is obviously effected by temperature but not to this extent. So, check out what O. fultoni SHOULD sound like under a given temperature on SINA, and cross reference it to a historical weather database for Nacogdoches, Texas. If the tempo and temperature is WAY off, it might indicate that the song belongs to V. micado. Obviously pair this information with other auxiliary information described in this post to make an accurate decision.
Finally, V. micado and Gryllus fultoni can sound very similar. They both have a dry chirp at similar frequencies that regularly trips over itself. V. micado is typically faster than G. fultoni, and when in doubt, a band filter will reveal that G. fultoni has a characteristic 2-3 ps/ch and V. micado will have 5-6 ps/ch.



Fig 4. A dry chirp that could be V. micado or G. fultoni . A band filter shows that the chirp is reliably 3 ps/ch, which is indicative of G. fultoni.


Xeno-canto observations for all three species and Strang’s Nature Inquiry post on V. micado were helpful here.


Gryllus pennsylvanicus | Gryllus fultoni
The song of Gryllus fultoni (Southern wood cricket) is inconsistent and trips over itself, thereby making it sometimes confusing to separate with V. micado. However, Gryllus pennsylvanicus (Fall field cricket) is the quintessential cricket. It will have the characteristic dry tone of Gryllus, but I’ve found that the tempo is more even-paced than G. fultoni. Basically the same case that I made for O. fultoni and V. micado. For the purposes of this project, I’ve found many more G. fultoni in our recordings than G. pennsylvanicus. G. pennsylvanicus’s geographic range is just on the edge of our sampling region.


Allonemobius tinnulus | Anaxipha tinnulenta
This issue didn’t appear until I was 1,250 recordings into annotating training data. The range map on SINA for Allonemobius tinnulus (Tinkling ground cricket) shows a range that is not within our sampling region, but the Song of Insects database begs to differ. Upon listening and reading about these two species it became clear they could not be identified by sound alone…uh oh. Thankfully, the naturalist records of Dr. Carl Strang came in handy yet again—Carl is a naturalist in Illinois whom I’ve never met, but his records on singing insects is a huge help for many of our Texas orthopterans whose ranges extend across Illinois and Texas. I’ll probably reference Carl’s naturalist blog—Nature Inquiries—a couple times throughout this page.
See this blog post. The note morphology can separate the two species, but only for high quality signals. This will leave out some low-quality signals but will at least help annotators capture high-quality signals from these two species for our CNN model.



Fig 5. The large notes are A. tinnulenta (Slow-tinkling trig), which are more horizontal with a downward tail and the smaller notes are A.tinnulus (Tinkling ground cricket), which do not have a pronounced horizontal portion and appear arched with a longer downward tail relative to the note size. Photo credit: Carl Strang, Nature Inquiries 2021).




Cycloptilum | Cyrtoxipha columbiana
Cycloptilum (scaly crickets) and Cyrtoxipha columbiana (Columbian trig) are similar sounding taxa that occur in the same frequency range (~6.4-6.9 kHz). C. columbiana has a song that is more melodic or chime-like than Cycloptilum’s silvery and dry song. However, this is not enough to reliably tell them apart in my opinion. To be safe I look at the waveform to count the pulse rate per chirp because it’s an easy tell. The key feature to look for: C. Columbiana has ~5 pulses per chirp (ps/ch) and Cycloptilum reliably has 2 ps/ch.



Fig 6. An image of a chirping species that occurs anywhere from ~5.5-6.6 kHz which could be C. Columbiana or Cycloptilum. Check the waveform, which will show an oscillogram to view signal change over time! Use a band filter to view the specific signal in question.





Fig 7. A close look at the pulse rate of this chirp—using a band frequency filter—shows 2 pulses per chirp (ps/ch). This is indicative of Cycliptilum.





Fig 8. Not the best image (I will update when I come across a better recording) but this is the filtered waveform of a chirp within the Cycloptilum/Cyrtoxipha frequency range that belongs to Cyrtoxipha. Notice that there is no clear 2 ps/ch pattern, rather there is ~5-6 ps/ch (ignoring the noise).


In eastern Texas, we have Cycloptilum squamosum and Cycloptilum comprehendens. Both have 2 ps/ch and occupy the same frequency range. Unfortunately, there is very little information about these two species. I’ve found 1 reference recording for each (please reach out if you have more examples!). It appears that C. comprehendens might have more of a two-step tempo than C. squamosum, but I know nothing about the variability of these two species’ songs due to the limited data that is available. For now, I annotate these songs as Cycloptilum. Not as specific as I’d like to get but it’s accurate, based on the current information and still speaks to the functional diversity present at our field sites.


Eunemobius carolinus | Eunemobius melodius | Eunemobius confusus | Anurogryllus arboreus
These species were actually quite simple to separate once I developed an ear for Orthoptera songs. Eunemobius carolinus (Carolina ground cricket) is the most common. This species is geographically widespread and calls loudly throughout the day and night.
First let’s discuss E. carolinus and E. melodius (Melodius ground cricket). E. carolinus should be a lot more common than E. melodius. It is a common species already, and E. melodius’s geographic range is just on the edge of our field sites. That being said I’ve come across both species in our recordings.
The most important identifier: E. carolinus’s song is VERY dry. The song of E. melodius follows its namesake—very melodic and bell-like, similar to a high-frequency Oecanthus. I’ve also found E. carolinus’s signal to be fuzzier than E. melodius, although this is probably because there’s more E. carolinus around to chorus all at once, creating a lot of reverberations around the signal.



Fig 9. An image of Eunemobius melodius’s song in the spectrogram across a 1-minute recording.


E. confusus (Confused ground cricket) and E. carolinus (Carolina ground cricket) both have a dry song. It’s sometimes tricky, because E. carolinus will pulsatee and sputter like E. confusus. However, E. confusus is true to its namesake. It sounds really confused—starting and stopping, sputtering - stopping for seconds on end before starting again; maybe a slight ticking at its start up. E. carolinus won’t do this—even if its song may pulsate and sputter, it still carries on without continuous stopping.



Fig 10. An example of E. confusus (top signal) and E. carolinus (bottom signal). While both having dry songs in similar frequency ranges, E. confusus is inconsistent and sputtering throughout. Both species names are positioned at the top of their signal.


There might be some debate about whether Anaxipha exigua (read below) singing ar low tempertaures could be mistaken for E. melodius. In most cases their frequency ranges should not overlap. *more on this to come - see this blog post!
Last, E. carolinus and Anurogryllus arboreus (Common short-tailed cricket) can sound similar—both give a dry trill. Their frequency ranges should not overlap, but just in case they do an easy identifier is E. carolinus’s sputtering and pulsating trill (almost drone-like) versus A. arboreus’s consistent trill. Also, A. arboreus is reported to only sing right after sunset (0.5-1 hour).
Here is a brief overview of these four species in order from lower to higher suspected carrier frequency:

All sing between 5.6-6.7 kHz.



A. arboreus: Dry and continuous trill. Does not pulsate or sputter. Sings immediately after sunset.
E. carolinus: Frequent singer. Drone-like trill that pulsates and sputters continuously.
E. melodius: Not very common. Melodic and bell-like trill that can start and stop again. Can be similar to A. exigua but isn’t reported to have the “chuwee” beginning and shouldn’t reach the frequency range of A. exigua.
E. confusus: Continuous sputtering and stopping. Trilling and stop lengths are inconsistent.

Here is a fantastic comparison of the ground singing orthopterans: link.


Anaxipha exigua | Neonemobius variegatus | Neonemobius cubensis
Please see the Nature Inquiries post one and two about these species. It does a better job than I can at describing the subtle sound differences between the species.
Basic things to remember: All three species crescendo—their songs start lower than their peak frequency and slowly pitch up as they sing to make a horizontal asymptote. A. exigua (Say’s trig) is common and LOUD. Many sources report it as being quite obnoxious with a bell-like sound. N. variegatus (Variegated ground cricket) and N. cubensis (Cuban ground cricket) are quieter and have a silvery sound. The key to A. exigua is that it crescendos like the other two species but at the start listen closely for a “chuwee” sound, similar to a motor starting up.
Here is a fantastic comparison of the ground singing orthopterans: link.

title: Welcome!
text:
Welcome!
This is a collaborative project through the Grames Lab at Binghamton Univeristy to restore a long-term passive acoustic monitoring (PAM) dataset to better understand spatial and temporal patterns of the nocturnal orthopterans (crickets and katydids) of eastern Texas.







How to use these docs
If it’s your first time annotating and identifying Orthoptera by their stridulation patterns (i.e., song), start with this brief background of the project and then continue to the Introduction to RavenPro page. This website is a collection of resources to help new and existing annotators learn Orthoptera ID, use RavenPro, and annotate acoustic signals well enough to train a convolutional neural network (CNN) for automated ID. Use the search tool on the site as needed, or the navigation menu for each page.


Project background
Orthoptera (crickets, katydids, grasshoppers, locusts) are declining more rapidly than other insect taxa and are an important part of soundscapes, the collective noises in an ecosystem that can indicate its health. Orthoptera provide numerous ecosystem functions and services including nutrient cycling, trophic support as food sources, entomophagy, and seed dispersal. Because they are sensitive to environmental change, they are declining more rapidly than other insect groups, with estimates reaching 2.1-2.7% per year (Welti et al. 2020). This sensitivity also makes them good bioindicators (Riede 1998, McNeil and Grozinger 2020) to be used as a tool for broader conservation management (Menz et al. 2013). Despite their importance to ecosystem function, there is limited consistent and long-term monitoring data for Orthoptera, especially for the nocturnal species (e.g. katydids and crickets).



Fig 1. A summarization of some ecosystem functions and services that Orthoptera provide.


We are leveraging a 25-year time series dataset of soundscape recordings – originally meant to collect amphibian calls—collected by USDA biologists in eastern Texas. We will use the dataset to measure the trends in orthopteran communities over the last two decades to build stronger conclusions about community change and suspected decline alongside other environmental drivers (e.g., climate and land use change).



Fig 2. The field sites in eastern Texas where recordings were captured nightly for 25 years.


Our objective is to apply a pre-trained convolutional neural network (CNN) model to automatically classify orthopteran songs as species ID in digital and analog recordings.



Fig 3. An example spectrogram of the recordings we are annotating for this project. Each instance of energy (lighter color in the image) is sound at a given frequency.


The total dataset is ~ 7,200 hours, but our goal is to taxonomically identify a subset of the data (a few hundred hours) to teach the CNN model automate classification. We will create the training dataset using the RavenPro sound analysis tool. The training data will feed into a pre-trained CNN network, BirdNet, originally developed for bird identification—both tools were developed by the K. Lisa Yang Center for Conservation Bioacoustics.
Oh…and recordings from 2000-2009 are in analog cassette format which we will digitize! When completed, this will be the largest consistent PAM dataset for Orthoptera in the world, and will hopefully inform conservation management and monitoring initiatives .



Fig 4. Just one of the eight boxes that are filled with PAM cassette tapes… yippee!

title: Annotations tutorial
text: This tutorial assumes that the user has general knowledge of RavenPro. If not, please see the Introduction to RavenPro page for more information. To start:

title: Annotations tutorial
text:
1. Box a call
Use the selection tool to draw a box around a suspected Orthopteran stridulation. Omit the reverberations and include only the strongest parts of the signal.



Figure 1. Select the Orthopteran signal at ~ 5kHz and press enter.


Let’s figure out how to ID this call at ~5-5.5 kHz. Open the Orthoptera Call Guide which is the first step one should take to ID a signal. This reference guide has all the possible stridulating Orthopterans in Eastern Texas.

title: Annotations tutorial
text:
2. Describe the sound
Box the signal. Play your selection using the Filtered Play function so that only the frequency range that is within the boxed signal is played. Describe the sound. Is it a chirp (or a chorus of chirps)—individual buzzy or chime-like notes, or is it a trill—a single and consistent note? It’s best to decide this by sound and by visually inspecting the signal morphology. Sometimes chirping species chorus—many chirps happening at once—resulting in the signal morphology resembling a trill. In this case it’s only possible to recognize the chorus as a chirping species by auditory recognition, so pay careful attention. Our selection appears to be a chorusing species—when zoomed, we can see many strong individual signals accumulating between ~5 and ~5.6 kHz.



Figure 2. Our selection seems to be many individual chirps. This is many individuals of the same species chorusing at once.

title: Annotations tutorial
text:
2. Consider the frequency range
We’ve established that our boxed signal might be described as many (chorusing) buzzy chirps that last ~0.5-1 second each. Now let’s consider the frequency. Open the Orthoptera Song Guide.
Look at the Frequency Column. Open the links for any species that fall close to the frequency range of our boxed signal—considering the min to max frequency, or middle and 95% frequency. This is why it’s important to box signals accurately—including too much noise in the selection will make it very difficult to narrow down an ID based on frequency and sound. Each species has a link to the Singing Insects of North America (SINA) database. There will be variation when comparing the SINA recordings to our own. In most cases, the reference recordings on SINA are taken in a prefect environment whereas our field recordings will have variation in sound and frequency range—keep this in mind. Base your ID on multiple resources (see the Resources page) and types of ID support (e.g., sound, frequency, pulse rate). This rule will vary—some species are easier to ID by sound than others.
Put it all together: the signal in question is a chirping species that is chorusing. It is within the range of 5-5.6kHz, and it is giving off buzzy ~0.5-1 sec signals. Based on sound we might surmise that it could be Orocharis saltator or Gryllus pennsylvanicus.




Figure 3. Two reference spectrograms of O. saltator (top) and G. pennsylvanicus (bottom) from SINA used to compare against our signal in RavenPro.


However, G. pennsylvanicus has a lighter, less buzzy sound than our signal and O. saltator, and typically occurs at a lower frequency. Therefore, we can be confident that there’s no other species this signal can belong to other than O. saltator.

title: Annotations tutorial
section: 3. Enter ID information in the selection table
text:
3. Enter ID information in the selection table
Enter our ID under the Annotation column. Since we’re confident in our ID, we don’t need a secondary ID in the Notes column. Make sure that the name in the Annotation column is consistent—‘Genus_species’ (i.e., Orocharis_saltator).



Figure 4. Once the signal is identified, enter the primary species ID as Genus_species in the Annotation column.

title: Getting started in RavenPro
text:
Raven Pro is a software program for the acquisition, visualization, measurement, and analysis of sounds developed by the K. Lisa Yang Center for Conservation Bioacoustics at the Cornell Lab of Ornithology. Open RavenPro, which will have an a desktop icon like this: 
RavenPro should open to a blank workbench (Fig 1).



Fig 1. Opening screen on the RavenPro software.


There are many components and configurations for the RavenPro software. Included in these docs are the main components that we’ll use. For a more detailed tutorial of RavenPro, please see its user manual.



Fig 2. The main components of RavenPro.



Importing sound files
Annotators will receive learning sets of recordings inside a hard drive titled Cricket Recordings/Annotations_S26. Each annotator will have a directory with their name. Inside their named directory will be a list of recordings specifically assigned to them. For now navigate to the directory learning_recordings with labeled directories t1-t4.
To open a recording, click file > open sound recordings and navigate to the directory with your training recordings—they’ll be .wav format (Figure 3).



Fig 3. Open sound files in RavenPro.


Do not alter any default settings. Click continue. The original file will show doubles of the recording, and the waveform and spectrogram. Uncheck channel 2 on the side panel. Note: sometimes channel 2 has a much stronger signal than channel 1. If this is the case use channel 2.


Spectrogram and waveform
The spectrogram is the primary panel that we’ll view when a sound file is played. The spectrogram represents the frequency of the calls (y-axis) across time (x-axis). The color of the call in the spectrogram represents the power (energy) emitted in the recording at each point in time. The color can be changed—black/white/gray tones might be the easiest to work with.
The waveform displays an oscillogram showing amplitude (y-axis) across time (x-axis). This will be extremely useful for similar sounding Orthopterans. We can use the oscillogram to view chirp and pulse rate—the time between chirps (ch/s) and between pulses in a single chirp (ps/ch) which might be important for IDs. More on this later!



Fig 4. Display of the spectrogram and waveform with the channel 2 and waveform unchecked. For easy viewing during the first pass of the recording it’s okay to uncheck the waveform and keep it unchecked until you need it.




Color and zoom settings
There are different colors available to view the spectrogram. The grayscale or jet (default) option might be the easiest/most consistent color to use.



Fig 5. Drop down menu for color options.


Zoom the spectrogram window as needed. This isn’t mandatory but is reccomended since some species might need to be boxed in sections if their calling is inconsistent; the same species’ signal spaced more than 3 seconds apart from each other.




Fig 6. Two modes of zooming the spectrogram and/or waveform. (1) click in the window (spectrogram or waveform); (2) use the zoom button in the top panel or bottom right corner of the RavenPro window. The |--| button in the bottom right window will reset the zoom to its default.




Selection table
Editing the selection table is critical for annotating acoustic signals for this project. (1) right click the empty space next to the table columns and choose add annotation column; (2) name one column Annotation and another Notes. Keep both case sensitive. Annotation will recieve your primary ID. Notes will receive the alternative ID (if applicable).
Click on the right of the selection table and choose Measurements. Add 95% Frequency to the table. The low and high frequency which corresponds to the species ID will vary depending on the person annotating. The 95% Frequency column will account for individual differences between annotators.



Fig 7. Editing the selection table for Orthoptera annotations.


If you need to delete a selection, right click the selection in the table and choose Clear Active Selections.


Play sound in RavenPro
The controls for playing sound are located on the top toolbars (Figure 2). Play will start playing the recording continuously until paused. Play Visible will play the entire frequency range within the time series window. As the sound plays, a line moves across the spectrogram and waveform. For more information see the RavenPro manual, but we will mostly use Play Visible and Filtered Play. Once a signal is boxed, we can use Filtered Play to omit any sound that occurs outside of our selected box and then when we select Play Visible, it will only play the boxed signal. This workflow is essentially the primary tools you will need to listen and isolate sound to make an accurate ID. We will revisit this on the Tutorial page.



Figure 8. Playback tool bar which is located at the top of the RavenPro window (Charif, Waak, and Strickman 2010). The volume setting is positioned next to the play settings.


Recordings can be quieter than the sample recordings online, that are used to ID. Its recommended to turn up the volume within RavenPro and keep the volume at a reasonable level on the computer so that you don’t blow your eardrums every time you switch between software!



Fig 9. Increase or decrease sound levels only within the RavenPro software.




Annotate acoustic signals
Use the selection tool to draw a box around an acoustic signal. The box should be drawn using the selection tool + located on the top toolbar.



Fig 10. Selection tool used to draw a box around an acoustic signal. Bonus: the pointer finger icon allows the user to select a boxed signal to edit its extent and position. The same thing can be accomplished by clicking the selection in the selection table.





Fig 11. An example of a boxed acoustic signal. Notice how tight I boxed the signal. Leave out the reverberations—the portion of the signal that fades as the energy dissipates. We’re interested in the primary signal that’s emitted by the Orthopteran stridulation.


Once a box is drawn around a signal, press enter. A popup box will appear—either press enter again and create an empty selection in the selection table, or directly enter the ID and alternative ID, if necessary, and then press enter to add to the selection table.



Fig 12. Selection pop-up that needs to be saved (press enter) to the selection table. Otherwise, once another selection is made, the previous one will disappear. To change this workflow, uncheck the option that says “Show this dialog whenever a selection is committed.


When entering an ID, put the primary ID in the Annotation column and the secondary ID—if there is one—in the Notes column. IDs should be formatted as Genus_species—case sensitive. If there are more than one alternative ID, format the entry Genus_species_or_Genus_species.



Fig 13. Proper formatting for an ID. This specific signal has no other species within the frequency range that sounds similar, so the Notes column is left empty.


At the lower frequencies the alternative ID might sometimes be frog. Some toad and Oecanthus species sound similar. If you’re unsure of the specific species it’s okay to only enter the genus. For instance, Oecanthus is almost always just entered as Oecanthus. The species in this genus have very similar stridulation patterns in the same frequency range. For more on this, continue to the Tutorial page.


Saving a selection table
Finally, to save a selection table navigate to file > Save "Sound 1" selection table (table 1) as and leave the name as default. The default should be the exact same name as the corresponding sound file but with ~Table.1.selections.txt attached to the end.



Fig 14. Save the selection table as the default name—the same name as its corresponding sound file. It’s important to check the directory to which the file is being saved. RavenPro will open random folders under Save in: .

title: ID Key
text:
Workflow key for singing orthopterans
If it helps, follow this key generally. No identification should be made solely on the frequency, sound, or morphology of the acoustic signal. Please use this workflow alongside the naturalist accounts available in the ID Help | Blog page or the Project Resources page.


Start: Annotate an acoustic signal
Draw a box around a call. Make sure the box covers only the dark regions (strongest signal) and avoids reverberations above or below the main energy signal. Example:



Fig 1. Draw a box around the acoustic signal, large enough to capture the signal but small enough to remove any noise.



Call type: Is it a chirp or a trill? Check the “Call Type” column in the Orthoptera Song Guide for examples.
a. If it’s a chirp, continue to  2. 
b. If it’s a trill, continue to 5. 
c. I’m not sure. Seek help → (jelias4@binghamton.edu)
Go to the Orthoptera Song Guide and find all chirping species within ~0.5-1 kHz of your upper or lower lower bounds of your frequency range (in kHz). Open their links—does it sound like the selection in RavenPro? Note the naturalist accounts in our ID Help | Blog pageand Project Resources. Note how different species sound—melodic, dry, sputtering, etc. There are minor differences that annotators should be in tune with that are unique to a species’s song, even though at first glance it might seem like many species trill or chirp identically based on the first listen, look, and comparison.
a. Yes, and there’s only one species in the frequency range that sounds like the RavenPro selection. Continue to 8. 
b. Yes, but there’s a couple species that sound very similar and are within the same frequency range. Continue to 3. 
c. No, none of them sound, look, or are within the frequency range of the RavenPro selection. Seek help → (jelias4@binghamton.edu)
Look at the chirps in the spectrogram between the two species on their links in the Orthoptera Song Guide. How many pulses are within a single chirp? Now filter the selection in the RavenPro oscillogram and try to measure how many pulses are within a single chirp. 
a. The pulse rate on the oscillogram is close enough to one species and different from the other. Identifiable! Continue to 8. 
b. I can’t make out the pulse rate, or it’s too similar between both species. Continue to 4. 
c. I don’t know how to filter the oscillogram to look at the pulse rate. Seek help → (jelias4@binghamton.edu). 



Fig 2. A band filter around a single acoustic signal can be zoomed in to analyze the number of chirps/second and the number of pulses chirp. See the Introduction to RavenPro page for help using the waveform/oscillogram.


Look for singing information between the links provided on the Orthoptera Song Guide, and other sources if they exist for those species—see the ID Help | Blog pageand Project Resources. Are there any additional key characteristics or information that helps separate species ID? 
a. Yes, I’m able to narrow down ID to a single species. Continue to 8. 
b. No. Continue to 9.
Go to the Orthoptera Song Guide and find all trilling species within ~0.5-1 kHz of the upper or lower bounds of your selection’s frequency range (in kHz). Open their links—does it sound like the selection in RavenPro? Check the ID Help | Blog page, especially for trill species 6 kHz and above.
a. Yes, and there’s only one species in the frequency range that sounds like the RavenPro selection. Continue to 8. 
b. Yes, but there’s a couple that sound very similar and are within the same frequency range. Continue to 6. 
c. Yes, there’s a couple species that sound the same, all around 2.7-3.4 kHz. The dreaded Oecanthus genus…. Continue to 7. 
d. No, none of them sound, look, or are within the frequency range of the RavenPro selection. Seek help → (jelias4@binghamton.edu)
Typically, we can’t use the oscillogram for trilling species but thankfully most trilling species don’t overlap in frequency. If they do overlap (or come close), are there any trilling characteristics across the links provided on the Orthoptera Song Guide, and other sources if they exist for those species—see the ID Help | Blog pageand Project Resources that help separate the similar species.  
a. Yes, I’m able to narrow down ID to a single species. Continue to 8. 
b. No. Continue to 9. 
Most trilling Oecanthus are too similar to reliably ID. Label as Oecanthus in the Annotation column (e.g., Genus). If the trill is below 3.0 kHz, label Oecanthus as the primary IDin the Annotation column and Neoscapteriscus_borellii in the Notes column as the secondary ID.
Label the primary species ID in the Annotation column in RavenPro (e.g., Genus_species).
Label the primary species ID in the Annotation column in RavenPro (e.g., Genus_species). Label the secondary species ID in the Notes column (e.g., Genus_species). 
a. Still unsure? Continue to 10.
Place a ? in front of the primary ID (e.g., ?_Genus_species) and record it in the lab notebook and/or seek help → (jelias4@binghamton.edu). The most important thing is that a box is accurately drawn around the acoustic signal.

title: About
text:
I am a PhD student at Binghamton University heading this project on Orthoptera bioacoustics. I’m a general ecologist, mostly nested in quantitative biology. I’m interested in applying what we know about ecological patterns and behavior (e.g., GIS data, bioacoustics, positive phototaxis) to improve monitoring—mostly for arthropods—to help conservation management.
Check out my website portfolio and please reach out if you would like to talk about the Orthoptera bioacoustics project, or anything else I have going on.

title: Analog digitization
text: A substantial portion of the long‑term PAM archive—~2,600 of ~7,000 total hours—was originally recorded on cassette tapes. Because cassette tapes are an inherently unstable analog medium, they degrade over time. This makes it urgent to digitize the remaining recordings before they reach a point where high‑fidelity transfer is no longer possible. Fully digitizing this 25‑year PAM dataset will save one of the few continuous acoustic records of nocturnal vocalizing insects. Such a dataset will provide baseline ecological knowledge essential for conservation management, long‑term monitoring, and understanding how nocturnal insect communities respond to land‑use and climate change.

title: Analog digitization
text:
Using the portable cassette player
We use portable cassette players to digitize the cassette tapes. These are handheld and seem to do a good enough job at preserving frequency with its corresponding acoustic signal and species.
The cassette player plays the tape in real time (e.g., if the tape is 30 minutes long, it will take 30 minutes to digitize) and records the output onto an sd card. Each cassette side is approximately 40 minutes. A 20-25 hour/week position should complete ~ 20 cassettes per week, give or take 1-2 cassettes. Double this number when running two cassette players at once, which is expected once you get used to the process. Below are some common features of the player:



Figure 1. Portable cassette player used to digitize recordings in MP3 format.





Figure 2. There is a small lip that opens the cassette player to insert a cassette tape.





Figure 3. The sd card is housed on the side of the cassette player with the on/off button.





Figure 4. Softly press the sd card to release it from the cassette player.





Figure 5. The sd card has a corresponding thumb drive to connect to a computer and view the recordings on RavenPro.

title: Analog digitization
text:
Digitization Steps

1. Record the metadata for each tape
One of the most important components of this project is organization. We need to account for every single day and sampling period. Record everything that you are doing, or need to remember in order to account for every tape (both sides). You will be supplied with an online datasheet and organized boxes to keep organized.




Figure 6. Each tape has the date, year, and site written on the tape and case. Keep these two things together at all times.


For each tape write down the following information in the project datasheet:

Cassette year-month-day
Digitized? (yes - once it is digitized)
Notes (if necessary)

This datasheet and other resources for the project can be found in the project’s google drive.


2. Insert the cassette tape
Insert the tape (thin side down) into the cassette player and make sure the tape is between the two brackets.



Figure 7. Insert the cassette tape between the brackets and ensure that the tape is fully fast forwarded or rewound.




3. Rewind or fast forward the tape to the beginning
Before playing the tape, make sure that the tape is fully rewound and fast forwarded. The tape roll on the right of the cassette will start when the play button is pressed.




Figure 8. The pictured cassette tape is ready to be played now that it’s been rewound to the beginning of a tape roll.




4. Press play and record
Press play. Wait until you here a voice that will say the day and time. You can adjust the volume on the top of the player, or use headphones. The headphone jack is next to the on/off button.



Figure 9. Press play and wait until you hear a voice indicating the date and time. Press record. If you don’t hear a voice or an environmental soundscape in the first couple minutes there’s a good chance that the tape is stuck. In this case scroll down for further instructions.


Once you hear the voice which indicates the date and time, immediately hold in the record button until you see REC on the right side of the screen. Ensure that the recorder is charged at all times. DO NOT start a recording at 1 bar of battery - plug it in and start the recording. If the recorder stops or dies mid-recording, you will need to start over - delete the partially digitized MP3 file. We want two recordings (front and back) per cassette.



Figure 10. Press record and make sure the “REC” indicator is flashing. Adjust the volume as needed and ensure the battery has more than one bar.


The tape will play for ~ 40-50 minutes. Maybe ~35 minutes of that will actually be passive acoustic monitoring (PAM) data and the rest will be left over tape. Once the end is reached, flip the tape around and repeat the process.


5. Verify and rename the recording
5a. I recommend running through no more than 4 cassette tapes (8 MP3 filts) before renaming the files and filling out the online datasheet. Attach the microsd card to the thumbdrive and connect it to a computer with RavenPro. 
This tutorial already assumes that the user knows the basics of RavenPro. If not, please see the Introduction to RavenPro section of these docs.
5b. Open the recording in RavenPro, which will be automatically saved in the microsd card as “TAPE##”.



Figure 11. Open the recording one by one in the RavenPro software to extract the metadata for each tape. In the image TAPE001 and TAPE002 are the front and back of one cassette tape.


Since the cassette tapes hold multiple days of data, the recording will have multiple indicators (the voice of the Orthopteran god that tells us the date and time in the recording). Each broadband signal spanning 0-10 kHz is likely the voice indicator.



Figure 12. Each broadband signal, spaced 1 minute apart is likely metadata for each date and time.


5c. Zoom in and listen to the first and last indicator to make sure all the dates listed on the tape/tape case are included. These date stamps should occur every minute in the recording.



Figure 13. Zoom in to listen to the date and time indicator.


5d. Once the recording has been verified, name the corresponding file as site_date#1_date#2 listed in the file.



Figure 14. The name format should resemble the ones in the image. P# indicates the site and the dates span from the earliest to latest on each individual tape.



IMPORTANT: It is absolutely crucial to use standard formatting, and that the dates listed in the file name match the data in the file. Things can get disorganized very quickly considering that we have the same date for multiple years and sites, and that the voice of the Orthopteran god does not explicitely say the year or site in the recording. (1) All cassettes stay with their corresponding case and (2) check the recording to make sure it was digitized properly before moving on to the next batch and/or recording the information in the datasheet.
Any discrepancies will result in multiple cassettes having to be re-digitized—that is if we are able to find what is missing. It would involve digging through multiple boxes filled with hundreds of cassette tapes.



6. Add the metadata in the datasheet and mark digitized on the cassette tape
Once the recording has been verified and correctly named, mark “yes” under “Digitized (y/n):” in your notes. Move on to the next cassette tape.
As a second form of verification and organization we will write the digitization date and the initials of the person that digitized the tape on the back of the case only after verifying that the recording we digitized properly and renamed, and the metadata added to the datasheet.



Figure 15. Mark the cassette tape as digitized, enter the metadata into the datasheet, and mark the tape as digitized.




7. Transfer files for long-term storage
Transfer the files from the cassette player thumb drive to the larger storage hard drive kept in the lab. Once you are sure that the files transferred completely, delete the files from the cassette play thumb drive.
All cassette tapes that are successfully digitized will be placed in their own separate box that will be organized by site #. The same will be done for cassettes that had issues. We will digitize all the cassettes for a site before moving on to the next site.

title: Analog digitization
text:
Issues with cassette tapes
Some of these cassette tapes will have issues. If this issues persist which results in the tape not being able to be digitized, (1) make sure the tape does not stay in the datasheet and especially make sure that this tape does not get marked as “yes” under “digitized? (y/n)” or on the tape itself; (2) insert a piece of paper in the case that says “issue” - and briefly describe the issue.



Figure 16. Some cassettes will already have degraded and will need further restoration steps.



a. Sticky tapes
Most commonly the cassette tapes might play very slowly, or might not play at all. If this occurs you could try fast forwarding or rewinding a couple seconds to unstick the tape or manually turning the tape a little. If the issue persists, mark the tape with a piece of paper detailing the issue and store it separate from the digitized tapes.


b. Issues opening the recording in RavenPro
i. The file is corrupt or unreadable. Before placing the cassette tape with others that have issues, try restoring the thumb drive. This issue is common if you don’t properly eject the thumb drive before removing it from the computer.
ii. RavenPro is having issues opening the file due to storage capacity. Try restarting RavenPro—this is often the fix.



Figure 17. An example of an error message that RavenPro might throw out when opening sound files.




8. Transfer cassette tapes for long-term storage
All cassette tapes that are successfully digitized will be placed in their own separate box that will be organized by site #. The same will be done for cassettes that had issues. We will digitize all the cassettes for a site before moving on to the next site.
